===== 10783 2026-09-15T09:51:20.618Z 5350
Definitions first, then the three questions that have hard answers in the tree, then the two you asked me to start. One of the facts below changes the picture on both the type checking and the speed.

## The words

- **Reshape**: take the elements of an array in order and lay them out in a different shape. `(2,3)⍴` of six numbers is a two-by-three matrix. Hsu's layout lives on this: the parameters are one flat vector of 4192 numbers and each weight matrix is a reshape of a slice of it.
- **Ravel** (`,`): the opposite, flatten any array into a vector in row-major order. `⊃,/,¨` in the program ravels nine gradient matrices and joins them into the one flat gradient vector.
- **Planes**: a rank-3 array is a stack of matrices; each matrix in the stack is a plane. The attention block is one plane per (document, head) pair, and `⍤2` means "do this to every plane".
- **Gather**: pick rows of a matrix by a list of indices. `wte[ids;]` takes the embedding row of every token in the batch.
- **Outer product** (`∘.f`): apply `f` to every pair from two vectors, giving a matrix. `ids∘.=⍳27` compares each token id with each of the 27 vocabulary indices, which is the one-hot matrix; `(⍳16)∘.≥⍳16` compares positions and is the causal mask.

## Ring, Field, and which specification

I search the in-repo `Specification/` tree, which is the later draft with the implementers' notes, not the frozen 1.0. On the algebraic library the draft's chapter is `advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex`, and its `Ring` and `Field` declarations are there as commented-out LaTeX, lines 1541 and 1761, never made normative. The shipped library has `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing` and an `AnyMultiplicativeRing` marker, nothing more; and, as the Fable review found, the shipped `RR64` does not even satisfy the spec's `AdditiveGroup` bound. On positional arguments, the same draft: nothing, in any chapter or in the parser.

## The `nat` parameters, and the fact that changes things

You have the intent exactly right, and there are two reasons your expectation is not met here, one of them new.

The first I gave: the specification says `nat` parameters are "instantiated at runtime", so they were never meant as compile-time constants that a code generator folds; the design is dimension checking, not dimension-driven optimization. I know of no paper on this specifically; the published type-system work from the team (the OOPSLA 2011 paper on modular multiple dispatch, in `research/README.md`) is about overloading, not sizes.

The second is in `repo-internals.md` and I should have led with it: the static type checker exists, in Scala, and the walk interpreter never runs it. The `walk` command turns it off, and the phase is a no-op, so the interpreter runs untyped and every "type error" we have ever seen from it is a run-time dispatch failure. The `compile` command turns the checker on. So the compile-time error you are asking about, a mismatched dimension refused before running, is exactly what the compiled path is for, and it is the path this project has characterized but not finished.

That also answers the class-loader question. The bytecode compiler lowers every type to a JVM reference type and emits a dispatch method per overloaded name; there is no place in it where size checks would be generated, because in the design they are the checker's job, ahead of code generation, and the checker is the part that runs only on that path.

## The fast path, and the walking skeleton

The narrow path you describe exists and has numbers. `compiled-path-gaps.md` measured the bytecode compiler against the interpreter on the constructs microGPT is made of: 6.8× on a scalar loop, 8.9× on object allocation and operator calls, numerics identical to the last digit. Its finding is that the gap is not code generation but the compiler's tiny prelude library, with a prioritized worklist. So the skeleton is: take C4's program and vocabulary, which are plain Fortress, push them through `fortress compile`, and close prelude gaps in the order the program hits them, with the interpreter kept as the debugging path and the goldens as the oracle. That gives both the static checker and the speed on the same road. Truffle on Graal would be a rewrite of the interpreter for a JIT it does not have today; it is a different, larger project and not the first step.

## The inventory you asked for

That is the ledger review, and your framing is the right one for it: not "what is broken" but "where does Fortress stand, area by area, against the languages you know, and which of its edges are design, unfinished implementation, or never built". I am launching a Fable worker on that now, over all 287 rows and the ten reports, with your questions as its brief; I review the draft here. It is the document the ordering of the next work should come out of.

On the history: DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three in 2006, and Fortress went on as a Sun Labs project until 2012, so "died for good reasons" is at least half right; the syntax and type machinery are what got built, and the compiler that would have made the parallelism pay is what did not. Hsu's critique lands on that same seam. As for training every model to write APL: the program in `apl/mg/` is nineteen lines and correct to the last bit, so the takeover has a proof of concept.
===== 10856 2026-09-15T10:06:06.559Z 2512
The inventory you asked for is done and published: https://claude.ai/artifact/Jk2FvveWzwDJmaq6wJFux8 (source `explorations/reviews/fortress-characterized.md`, on main). A Fable worker drafted it from all 286 ledger rows and the tree's reports; I read its opening and its options section against what I know and found nothing to correct.

What it gives you, in the order you will want it:

- **One page on what Fortress actually is here.** Two executions of one language: the interpreter with the type checker off, and the compiler that runs the checker, is 6.8 to 8.9× faster on the shapes microGPT is made of, and lacks a 592-line prelude. Parallelism, syntax extension and the notation surface in a paragraph each, every sentence with a row number.
- **Nine areas, each a table.** The concept a Scala, Swift, Kotlin or Rust programmer brings; what Fortress has by design; what the implementation does; the rows behind it. Numerics, arrays and the algebraic traits, generics and overloading, functions, collections and strings, modules, parallelism, syntax extension, tooling.
- **The mismatches, named.** Nine concepts from those languages with no counterpart here (point-free code, coercions, shadowing, pattern matching, sequential-by-default iteration, among them) and ten Fortress has that they lack (juxtaposition, declarable Unicode operators, sized types, symmetric multiple dispatch, big operators, contracts, parallel by default, syntax extension).
- **The rows classified.** 88 defects the revival could fix, 74 design limits no fix changes, 20 never-built parts of the design, 103 verified capabilities. The revival worklist checked against the 113 rows added since it was derived: its top items stand, ten small ones join it.
- **Five options for the next work, evidence for and against, no recommendation.** The compiled path for microGPT as a walking skeleton, which is the only option with a measured multiplier behind it and whose first two probes are named; the vocabulary swap, done but for the check runs; the ledger split, which this document began; further APL ground, closed by your decision; and five one-line interpreter fixes that de-risk everything else.

Two of your questions from this morning are answered in it with the same evidence I gave you: the static checker that would refuse a mismatched dimension exists and runs only on the compiled path, and the compiled path is where speed lives too. The document says so under option 1 without recommending it. The ordering is yours.

===== 11020 2026-09-15T10:45:07.996Z assistant 3679
Answers by item, then what is running.

**Ring, Field, and the `RR64` finding.** These are names for what a set of values can do. An additive group: you can add, subtract, and there is a zero. A ring: an additive group where you can also multiply, with a one. A field: a ring where you can also divide by anything but zero. Integers form a ring, reals form a field, matrices of a given size form a ring but not a field. The point of the traits is that once a type declares which of these it is, everything written in terms of the operations comes for free. The finding: the specification's array chapter writes its element bound as `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, and the shipped `RR64` is not declared to satisfy it, so a function written the spec's way refuses real numbers (probe `v04b_groupbound.out.0`); the bound that works is `T extends Number`, which is not algebra but a name. That is the first thing to fix in the layer you want. It is now in `FACTS.md`.

**"Fleshing out the standard library."** Recorded as your position. One question only you can answer, and I have not assumed the answer: the standing rule is that `Library/` is never modified, and this direction reads as modifying it. The alternative is building the algebraic layer in our own tree, over the shipped traits, which is what every run so far has done. Worklist item 4 is literally "unseal the linear-algebra layer", five rows. Say which.

**The checker in the interpreter.** It is not on the ledger as a fix, and neither of us missed a row: the nearest is row 69, which records that `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude and so is not an oracle for interpreter programs. Making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which falls under worklist item 2 and was never named on its own. It is named now, in `FACTS.md` and `POSITIONS.md`.

**Performance.** Recorded as your priority in `POSITIONS.md`, in your words. One correction to the record's honesty: that boxing is the cause of the ceiling is an inference from `repo-internals.md` (`RR64` lowered to a runtime object, no primitive arithmetic emitted), not a measurement. A one-day probe would make it one: the same scalar loop hand-written in Java over `double[]` beside the compiled Fortress loop, on this host. I have not launched it.

**The knowledge base.** `explorations/coordinator/`: `README.md` (the load order and the rules), `FACTS.md` (established facts by area, each with its source), `POSITIONS.md` (your decisions, what you already know, how you want to be spoken to). `CLAUDE.md`, which every session loads automatically, now points at it, and so does the handover. A fact enters in the same commit as the work that establishes it; nothing in it is restated to you unless it changes. This is the mechanism for surviving compactions: the summary can lose it, the tree cannot.

**The swap is in.** The focused base stands on its own vocabulary, `FlatArrays2`: 35 declarations against C4's 38, six of them with shared dimension names, thirteen agreeing `nat`s where C4 had thirty agreeing on nothing. Forward pass byte-identical, smoke 40 of 40, and the mismatch probe caught all seven wrong-shape calls at the call, as the shared names promise. One line is yours: the elementwise `×` and `/` cannot state shape agreement in the index-generic form (the interpreter refuses the two declarations side by side), only as three per-rank declarations each, taking the api from 35 to 39. Algebra stated or four fewer lines; either is one word from you.

The two recorded check runs on the new vocabulary are going now, pool 1 then pool 4; the cost row and the report follow.

A fork is a point where the work can go two or more ways and the choice changes what gets built afterwards. The plan reserves two of them for you. A worker is not allowed to pick either on its own, because the rungs it would build afterwards depend on the pick.

**Fork one: the array representation.** The compiler world has no array types at all. To add `Array`, `Vector`, `Matrix` there, someone must decide what an array is underneath: a library object over `get` and `put`, as the interpreter has it, or a JVM `double[]` with unboxed elements, which is where the six-fold cost of boxing lives. Every array name in the compiler prelude follows from that choice. The plan wants a written sketch of the design before the choice, and no sketch exists yet.

**Fork two: `nat` checking.** Sizes in types, like `Vector[\RR64, 16\]`, are `nat` parameters. The type checker does not implement them at all. It crashes on the first one. Until it does, the sized-array vocabulary cannot pass the checker, and the static shape checking the design promises exists nowhere. The choice is how to build it: inside the checker directly, or first as a shadow prototype beside the tree, the way the template fix was proved.

**Why this matters for batch 2.** All eighteen components of the two microGPT programs stop at the same place, on the names `Array`, `Char`, `Vector` and `ImmutableArray`. Those names sit behind fork one. So no batch of small rungs moves microGPT until fork one is decided. Batch 2 is "fork-free": three rungs that need neither decision. It keeps the machinery running and clears a few test files, but the real path runs through the forks.

That is why item 5 of the list proposes starting the array sketch and the `nat` prototype now, as worker sessions beside the batch. They prepare the decisions. They do not take them.

You are right about the feature, and the call itself never conflicts. `mask + scores` picks the plane-wise `+`, `x + 1.0` picks the scalar one, and the program runs. That is why it works on a warm cache. The refusal is not at the call. It is at load time, from a check the language runs over every pair of overloads before any call happens.

**What the two operators are.** The mask is a matrix, T by T. The attention scores for all heads are a 3-D array, heads by T by T. "Mask plus scores" adds the matrix to every plane of the 3-D array. The library's `+` only adds two things of the same type, matrix plus matrix. So C4 declares its own `+` for matrix plus 3-D array, and its own `+` for array plus scalar, because the library has no scalar extension for float arrays either. Both are C4's, both are generic: the first has size parameters, the second an index-type parameter.

**Why the language refuses the pair.** Fortress wants every pair of overloads to be unambiguous for every possible argument, including arguments of types nobody has written yet. For two overloads it cannot order, it demands one position where the parameter types are declared disjoint. Disjointness is not automatic between two traits, because some later type could extend both. It exists only where a trait says `excludes`. Nothing in the library says a number is not a 3-D array. So in the pair (array, number) against (matrix, 3-D array), no position is provably disjoint, and the check refuses. That is the interpreter's message, word for word: at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types.

**The letter of the specification is worse.** It says overloads that carry static parameters must carry the same ones. That rule alone forbids C4's two `+` from coexisting, whatever their types. The specification never finished the theory of overloading generic functions and closed the door instead. The reviewer left open whether the library's own `+` even counts under that sentence.

**So your intuition is right and the language is unfinished.** A mathematician assumes a scalar is not an array. The library never told the language so. The correction that honours your point is in the library, not in C4: declare that the numeric types and the array types exclude each other, and C4's declarations pass as written, zero lines changed. I have added exactly that as a fourth route for the worker to probe, ordered first if it passes. The mask-as-object route and the interpreter-check route stay as fallbacks.

trait AdditiveGroup[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\] extends AnyAdditiveGroup
    getter zero(): T = self - self
    opr +(self, other: T): T
    opr -(self, other: T): T = self + (-other)
    opr -(self) : T = self.zero - self
end

(** Place holder for exclusions of MultiplicativeRing **)
trait AnyMultiplicativeRing end

(** Multiplicative ring using TIMES and juxtaposition.
    Define opr TIMES; juxtaposition is defined in terms of TIMES. **)
trait MultiplicativeRing[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]
        extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    getter one(): T
    opr TIMES(self, other:T): T
    opr juxtaposition(self, other:T): T = self TIMES other
    (** Exponentiation need only deal with natural exponents. **)
    opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral): T
end

Your pattern match is a sound one. It's the same one the team made: Fortress's algebra traits play the part of Haskell's numeric classes. Here's the math with small numbers first, then your two ideas.

**The math, concretely:**
- **Dot product.** Multiply two lists pair by pair and add up the results. `[1, 2, 3] · [4, 5, 6]` = 1×4 + 2×5 + 3×6 = 32.
- **Matrix product.** Each entry of the result is the dot product of one row on the left with one column on the right. With A = `[[1, 2], [3, 4]]` and B = `[[5, 6], [7, 8]]`:
  - A·B = `[[19, 22], [43, 50]]`. The top-left entry is (1, 2)·(5, 7) = 5 + 14 = 19.
  - B·A = `[[23, 34], [31, 46]]`. So the order matters: A·B isn't B·A.
- **Shapes must match in the middle.** A 2×3 matrix times a 3×4 matrix gives a 2×4. A 2×3 matrix times a 2×3 isn't defined.
- **Additive group:** a set with a `+` that has a zero, gives every element a negative, and doesn't care how you group the terms: (a+b)+c = a+(b+c).
  - The integers are one. The numbers 0, 1, 2 and up are not, because they have no negatives.
  - Matrices of one shape are one: you add entry by entry, the zero matrix is all zeros, and you negate each entry.
- **Ring:** an additive group that also has a multiplication. That multiplication has a "one", doesn't care how you group the terms, and spreads over addition: a·(b+c) = a·b + a·c.
  - The integers are one.
  - Square matrices of one size are one too. Their "one" is `[[1, 0], [0, 1]]`, the identity matrix.
  - Non-square matrices are not, because A·A isn't even defined for them.
- **Why the library cares.** The traits are promises the library relies on.
  - `SUM` of an empty list gives the type's zero, which only an additive group promises.
  - Steele's ICFP talk splits a sum across processors. That's safe only because `+` doesn't care how you group the terms, and the trait is the promise of that.

**Your square-matrix idea.** Yes, that's exactly this kind of clause, with a condition on sizes:
```
trait Matrix[\T, nat n, nat m\]
    extends MultiplicativeRing[\Matrix[\T,n,m\]\]
    where { n = m }
```

**Your diagonal.** Two diagonal matrices of one size multiply by multiplying their diagonals entry by entry: diag(2, 3) · diag(4, 5) = diag(8, 15). There the order doesn't matter, so diagonals form a ring whose multiplication behaves like numbers'.
